overview: Turners Automotive Group is New Zealand's largest buyer and seller of used vehicles, operating an integrated 'flywheel' ecosystem spanning Auto Retail (Turners Cars/Buy Right Cars auction and dealership network), consumer and commercial Finance (Oxford Finance/Turners Finance), Insurance (Autosure), a growing Servicing & Repairs mobile mechanic business, and a non-core Credit Management (EC Credit) debt-collection unit. The company operates a national branch network from Whangarei to Invercargill (33 sites, 18 company-owned) and is dual-listed on the NZX and ASX with fiscal year ending 31 March.

business_model.summary: Turners generates revenue from vehicle sales margins (owned and consigned/auction stock), interest income on a directly-originated consumer/commercial finance book, insurance premiums (motor, loan protection, life, MBI) largely sold at the point of vehicle sale, and fee income from servicing/repairs and third-party debt collection. The 'flywheel' strategy is designed so each vehicle sale creates cross-sell opportunities into higher-margin, more recurring Finance and Insurance products, lifting overall transaction economics and customer lifetime value.
business_model.customer_type: Primarily B2C (used vehicle buyers/sellers, consumer finance and insurance customers) with B2B elements (independent dealer/broker loan and insurance origination, commercial/trucks & machinery vehicle sales, corporate debt-referral clients)
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand-only operations (Auto Retail network Whangarei to Invercargill); dual-listed on NZX and ASX but no Australian trading operations

main_competitors: MTF Finance (Motor Trade Finance, dealer-owned finance network)
Avanti Finance / other non-bank consumer lenders
Tower/AA Insurance and other motor insurers
competitive_position.market_position: New Zealand's largest buyer and seller of used vehicles (41,000+ units sold FY26), with Finance loan book of $566m gross receivables and 200,000+ active insurance policies; scale leader as the number of registered NZ motor vehicle traders has fallen ~27% from a 2017 peak

moat_factors.description: Combining vehicle retail, finance and insurance at point of sale lifts transaction margins and is difficult for single-line competitors to replicate quickly
National branch network and diversified owned/consigned stock sourcing gives resilience and buying power that shrinking independent dealer numbers cannot match
Voted New Zealand's Most Trusted Used Vehicle Dealership seven years running; long-running 'Tina'/'Beep Beep' advertising campaign drives both sourcing leads and retail sales
In-house finance origination platform and years of loan performance data support arrears (2.5%) running well below the ~5.6% industry average
Inaugural $200m public securitisation warehouse (Oct 2025) reduced funding costs and capital intensity, a scale advantage smaller lenders lack

weaknesses: Auto Retail (used-vehicle wholesale/retail margin) is inherently cyclical and exposed to consumer discretionary spending
Finance book concentrated in automotive-linked consumer lending, correlating credit losses with the same macro cycle that hits vehicle sales
EC Credit (Credit Management) is being flagged for divestment after a goodwill write-down, reflecting a non-core, structurally challenged asset
Reliant on continued access to wholesale/securitisation funding markets to grow the loan book
New Zealand-only revenue base with no geographic diversification to offset a domestic downturn

growth_drivers: Branch network expansion - 15 planned new Auto Retail branches (four new plus two replacement branches in development for FY28) targeting rollout economics proven in Christchurch (+22% locally sourced units after opening three new branches)

Finance book growth (+27% YoY to $566m in FY26) via network-originated lending, direct-to-consumer and broker channels, a new unsecured lending product, and improved funding capacity from banking syndicate and securitisation facilities

Insurance growth through digital/direct-to-consumer distribution, new distribution partners (VTNZ, Gaspy, Quashed), and a repositioned Mechanical Breakdown Insurance product targeting the underserved private-to-private vehicle sale market

Turners Servicing & Repairs (rebranded from MyAutoShop) build-out - New Zealand's largest mobile mechanic network, targeting a $3 billion NZ servicing and repairs market opportunity and mirroring the Auto Retail footprint
Continued wholesale-to-retail sourcing mix shift and growth in the commercial (damaged/end-of-life, Trucks & Machinery) business, which is less sensitive to consumer sentiment
Structural industry tailwind from shrinking registered dealer numbers (down ~27% from the 2017 peak) consolidating share toward scaled operators like Turners
Improving capital effectiveness - securitisation warehouse cut Turners' capital requirement on receivables from 8% to 1.4%, freeing capital for redeployment into Finance growth
Potential EC Credit Management divestment to sharpen focus and capital allocation on the core automotive ecosystem

business.description: Vehicle sourcing costs, import volumes (affected by Clean Car Standard policy) and consumer demand swing margins materially; FY26 saw a soft first half with tight margins before a strong second-half recovery

business.risk: Competitive pressure from online marketplaces and value dealers
business.description: Trade Me Motors, Facebook Marketplace and value-focused rivals (e.g., 2 Cheap Cars) compress margins and shift lead origination online, pressuring stock turn industry-wide
Referral volumes fell as corporate clients paused referrals during system implementations; a $7.5m goodwill write-down was taken in FY26 and the business is now positioned for potential divestment

financial.risk: Interest rate / funding cost exposure on the finance book
financial.description: Oxford Finance funds a $566m loan book via securitisation warehouses and bank syndicate debt; margin depends on cost of funds relative to loan yields, though ~85% of borrowings are now hedged
Consumer arrears (2.5% at FY26) are well below the 5.6% industry average but could deteriorate if unemployment or interest rates rise; unsecured lending is a newer, less-seasoned product
Continued loan book growth depends on ongoing capital markets access; the October 2025 public securitisation was Turners' inaugural deal and reduced but did not eliminate refinancing/rollover risk

regulatory.risk: Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act (CCCFA) and lending law changes
regulatory.description: Affordability and disclosure requirements directly affect approval rates, loan origination volumes and compliance costs in Oxford Finance; historical CCCFA tightening reduced approval rates and required stricter provisioning across the NZ consumer lending industry
Non-compliance risk carries potential Commerce Commission fines and reputational damage that could depress loan originations and vehicle sales

regulatory.risk: Vehicle emissions and Clean Car Standard policy changes
regulatory.description: Changes to import rules affect the supply and mix of used vehicles available to source; recently announced relaxation to the Clean Car Standard is expected to ease import supply constraints

macro.risk: New Zealand consumer discretionary spending / consumer confidence
macro.description: Vehicle purchases are a large, deferrable discretionary spend; FY26 results were shaped by a soft first-half consumer environment before a second-half recovery, and April 2026 trading was again subdued following the Iran-US conflict shock
Affects both consumer affordability for vehicle finance and Turners' own cost of funds; a falling-rate environment has been supportive of demand and margins in FY26
Import volumes (down 13.5% YoY in 1H26) affect stock availability and pricing; NZD/JPY and NZD/AUD exchange rates influence landed vehicle costs

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ used car market is forecast to grow at roughly a 5-6% CAGR through 2031, with the organised/scaled dealer segment gaining share from independents as registered dealer numbers keep declining (down ~27% since the 2017 peak, lowest since 2012); electric/hybrid vehicle mix is rising (14.2% of Turners' FY26 sales, up from 11.9%)
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderately-high - Auto Retail margins and volumes are sensitive to consumer confidence and discretionary spending, though Finance and Insurance are more annuity-like and provide counter-cyclical earnings stability; management explicitly notes 'Finance and Insurance keep building... they don't stop when a car yard gets quiet'
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High and two-sided - lower rates support consumer vehicle affordability and finance demand while raising net interest margin pressure on funding costs; ~85% of Oxford Finance borrowings are hedged to reduce earnings volatility
key_input_costs: Cost of funds for the finance book (securitisation and bank funding)
Branch property and staff costs for network expansion

recent_developments.event: Turners raised FY26 NPBT guidance to approximately $63m (from $60m) on stronger summer trading, record vehicle margins and record January/February lending months, while flagging a $7-9m goodwill write-down related to EC Credit
Investor Day: management set a new medium-term NPBT target of $100 million by FY31, and confirmed the FY28 $65m NPBT target is on track to be achieved a year early in FY27

Completed inaugural $200 million public securitisation warehouse term-out (BNZ-funded, 13 investors from NZ and Australia), cutting Turners' capital requirement on the securitised receivables from 8% to 1.4% and lowering funding costs
New syndicated banking facilities signed, increasing receivables funding capacity to support FY31 growth ambitions

Record normalised NPBT of $63.2m (+16%), revenue of $451.2m (+9%), normalised NPAT of $45.6m (+18%), reported NPAT of $38.2m (including a $7.5m non-cash EC Credit goodwill write-down); loan book grew 27% to $566m; full-year dividend raised 14% to 33.0 cps

Iran-US conflict-driven geopolitical shock softened consumer sentiment in late March 2026, with April 2026 Auto Retail trading described by management as subdued - the same 'tough macro' playbook used in FY24/FY25 has been reapplied (selective buying, smaller/cheaper vehicle mix)

Three new Christchurch Auto Retail branches opened and reached full operational capacity; commercial branches added in Dunedin and Napier; 'Tina 2.0' brand campaign (launched May 2025, $5.1m media spend) won multiple advertising awards and lifted sourcing leads and units sold
EC Credit Management (formerly Debtworks/EC Credit Control) positioned for potential divestment over the medium term after being deemed non-core to the automotive ecosystem strategy

Rebrand of MyAutoShop to Turners Servicing & Repairs completed; expanded VTNZ partnership (pre-purchase inspections, WoF Wizard tool) and launched new Mechanical Breakdown Insurance product for the private-to-private vehicle market

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Report / March 2026 Investor Day

items.notes: Management now expects to hit the previously FY28 NPBT target a year early, in FY27, on the strength of FY26 momentum
New medium-term target announced at the March 2026 Investor Day, following successive multi-year targets (FY24 $45m and FY25 $50m) that were each beaten a year ahead of schedule
Stated as the anchor for the Group's capital allocation framework; capital released from securitisation is being redeployed to fund Oxford Finance growth
FY26 full-year dividend of 33.0 cps, up 14% on FY25, a ~10.5% CAGR over the past 12 years; Dividend Reinvestment Plan continues

items.target: 15 planned new Auto Retail branches (4 new + 2 replacement in development for FY28)
items.notes: FY27 flagged as a year of 'building and preparing rather than opening'

guidance.management_commentary: Chair and CEO stated the business has 'performed well in a down cycle and will perform even better in an upcycle,' citing a deeply integrated platform that is 'genuinely difficult to replicate.' Management flagged renewed consumer softness in late March/April 2026 following the Iran-US conflict shock but said the same 'tough macro' playbook used successfully in FY24 and FY25 (selective buying, smaller/cheaper vehicle mix, cost discipline) has been redeployed, while Finance and Insurance are described as 'annuity businesses' that provide earnings resilience through the cycle.

bull_case: Track record of beating self-set multi-year NPBT targets a year early (FY24, FY25, and likely FY27), lending credibility to the new $100m FY31 target implying ~50%+ growth from FY26's $63.2m

Flywheel model captures rising per-transaction economics as Finance and Insurance cross-sell penetration increases, with Finance loan book growth (27% YoY) delivering strong operating leverage and industry-leading credit quality (2.5% arrears vs 5.6% industry average)
Structural tailwind from shrinking independent dealer competition (registered dealers down ~27% since 2017) consolidates market share toward scaled, well-capitalised players like Turners

Improved funding structure (inaugural $200m public securitisation, new syndicated banking facilities) lowers cost of capital and capital intensity, supporting growth without proportionate equity dilution

Diversified, resilient earnings base with growing servicing/repairs and insurance annuity-like revenue cushioning cyclical Auto Retail swings, plus a rising, fully-imputed dividend (33 cps FY26, +14% YoY, ~10.5% 12-year CAGR)
bear_case: Auto Retail remains the largest earnings driver and is directly exposed to NZ consumer discretionary spending; renewed softness after the March 2026 Iran-US conflict shock shows how quickly sentiment can turn

Valuation already prices in continued execution - shares trade at a premium P/E versus NZ retail/finance peers, with recent commentary noting margin compression (net margin 9.3% to 8.5% TTM) and cash flow that lags reported earnings due to non-cash items and loan book growth absorbing cash
Regulatory risk from CCCFA and consumer credit law changes could tighten approval rates and raise compliance costs in Oxford Finance, a key growth engine

Credit and funding market risk - a $566m and growing loan book funded substantially through securitisation and bank facilities is exposed to a rise in wholesale funding costs or a tightening in credit markets, and consumer arrears could rise in a weaker labour market

EC Credit Management's structural decline (goodwill write-down, falling referral volumes) and pending divestment signal that not every segment of the diversified model is performing, and disposal proceeds/timing are uncertain
